questions.stem: Dr. Domagk is investigating the treatment of Staphylococcus aureus with a new compound. The compound is under heavy criticism because it does not appear to kill bacteria in vitro, but Dr. Domagk thinks it will work because it improves survival in S. aureus-infected mice. He is planning to do a study to prove that the new antibiotic should be used to treat S. aureus infections. In order to prove his theory, he needs a study design that provides the strongest evidence for causation.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate study design?
questions.explanation: Randomized controlled trial Randomized controlled trial is the correct answer because it is the strongest design in terms of establishing causation, since participants are randomized to treatment. Due to randomization, measured and unmeasured confounders should be equally distributed among the groups. An ecological study is the weakest design in terms of causation, because no inferences can be made about individuals from this design which involves aggregate data. Case– control and prospective cohorts are observational studies, and as such at risk for confounding and selection bias since treatment was not randomized. Meta-analyses combine the results of multiple studies and thus are not used to analyze data from individuals in order to establish causation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q48

questions.stem: A new diagnostic test has been developed for Lyme disease. Stored specimens from 1000 patients were tested with the new method, 80 of whom had previously been found to have Lyme disease by enzyme immunoassay/Western blot. The new test gave positive results in 60 of the previously identified individuals with Lyme disease, and gave positive results in 40 persons who were not previously identified with Lyme disease.
questions.lead_in: What are the sensitivity and positive predictive value of the new test compared to enzyme immunoassay/Western blot?
questions.explanation: 75% and 60% The data from this comparison is shown below in table format, based on the information provided: Test Result EIA/Western Blot + EIA/Western Blot - Positive 60 40 Negative 20 880 Based on these results the sensitivity = 60/80 = 75%. The positive predictive value = 60/100 = 60%.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q46

questions.stem: A survey is done to identify patients infected with hepatitis C virus in a community. Forty of the 1000 individuals surveyed in the community are found to be seropositive for HCV .
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate definition?
questions.explanation: Prevalence Prevalence is the correct result because the 1000 individuals were surveyed in the community, so this represents both new (incident) and preexisting HCV infection, and therefore prevalence. Incidence is not correct because an assay would have to be done to identify only newly infected individuals, which was not the case. Positive predictive value, sensitivity, and positive likelihood ratio are characteristics of diagnostic tests and therefore incorrect.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q47

questions.stem: Dr. Smith has performed a small study looking at the association of St. John’s wort with recurrent shingles. She has found a positive association and attempted to publish the paper. One of the reviewers is suggesting that this finding may have occurred due to chance alone.
questions.lead_in: What type of error is this?
questions.explanation: Type I Type I error is the type of error that occurs when the null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected (in reality there was no association, but by chance a positive result was found). Alpha is the significance level, the probability of making a type I error. Type II error (also called β) is the opposite – the null hypothesis of no association was accepted, but there truly was a difference in results. Confounding bias is due to an additional factor that distorts the relationship between an outcome and exposure.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q46

questions.model_answer: a) An acceptable multidrug regimen established with DOT arranged; clinical improvement; comorbidities (e.g., HIV) managed; drug-resistant TB not suspected; and a home setting where isolation can be maintained while still infectious. b) (1) Stay home, no work/school/public places; (2) no visitors, especially no new contacts (infants, immunocompromised); (3) sleep in a separate, well-ventilated room; (4) cover cough / wear a mask when others are present. c) Airborne isolation may stop when the patient is clinically improving on ≥2 weeks of effective therapy with drug-susceptible TB and has three consecutive negative AFB smears (MDR/rifampin-resistant cases require negative cultures). d) Case-control design principles: (1) observational; (2) subjects selected by outcome (cases with disease vs. controls without); (3) compare past exposure to a risk factor between the two groups. e) (1) Efficient/cheaper and quicker with fewer subjects; (2) suited to rare diseases or long-latency outcomes and can assess multiple exposures. f) Odds ratio. g) Biologic MOA/associated infections: anti-TNF (etanercept/infliximab/adalimumab) — TB reactivation; rituximab (anti-CD20) — HBV reactivation; tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R) — zoster, NTM, PJP; natalizumab (anti-α4) — PML; eculizumab (anti-C5) — Neisseria; belatacept (CTLA-4 Ig) — PTLD; fingolimod — severe herpesvirus infections.
questions.beyond_mandell: Discharge/home-isolation criteria and when to stop airborne precautions are from the Canadian TB Standards; case-control epidemiology and the biologic MOA/infection list are from general epidemiology and pharmacology references, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Criteria to release from hospital: DOT arranged; Acceptable tx regimen has been established; Comorbidities/medical conditions have been managed eg HIV; Home isolation is possible while still infectious eg first 2 weeks of tx; Clinical improvement; Drug resistant TB is not suspected
Elements for home isolation: Canadian TB standards
When isolation can be stopped: Suspect TB cases: Airborne precautions may be discontinued if three successive samples of sputum (spontaneous or induced) are negative on smear unless TB is still strongly suspected and no other diagnosis has been made. Confirmed TB cases - Smear negative, culture +, drug susceptible: patient has clinical evidence of improvement + evidence of adherence to at least 2 weeks of effective therapy; may be discharged to home isolation for the period requiring airborne precautions provided there is clinical improvement, drug-resistant TB is not suspected no contraindication for home isolation. Smear positive, culture +, drug susceptible: clinical evidence of improvement, evidence of adherence to at least 2 weeks of effective multidrug therapy based on the known antibiotic sensitivity of the patient's organism, 3 consecutive negative AFB sputum smears, same home isolation criteria. Multi-drug resistant TB cases and those with mono-resistance to rifampin (RMP): should have 3 consecutive negative sputum cultures after six weeks of incubation prior to discontinuing airborne precautions
a. Three essential principles of design: observational; two groups are compared between each other, one with the outcome/disease, the other without the outcome/disease; assess whether there is a statistically significant difference in the rates of exposure to a defined risk factor between the groups
b. Two advantages compared to cohort study: Less expensive, shorter to conduct, requires comparatively few subjects, allows multiple exposures or risk factors to be examined; Allows rare diseases/those with long latency to be examined
c. Statistical measure: Odds ratio
MOA and infections associated with biologics: Rituximab – antibody to CD-20 on B-cells causing B cell depletion. Associated with HBV reactivation. Tocilizumab – antibody to IL-6 receptor used to treat RA. Associated with Herpes Zoster, PJP and atypical mycobacterial infection. Ustekinumab (stelara) – antibody to IL-12 and IL-23 to treat plaque psoriasis. Nothing specific. Belimumab – antibody to B lymphocyte stimulator used to treat SLE. Cocci and CMV pneumonia reported. Abatacept – CTLA-4 Ig blocks CD28 T cell costimulation, used to treat RA. No specific infections risks identified. Belatacept – CTLA-4 IG blocks CD28 costimulation. Associated with PTLD. Natalizumab – inhibits leukocyte chemotaxis, used to treat MS. Associated with PML. Fingolimod – prevents lymphocyte movement out of lymph nodes, used to treat MS. Associated with life threatening herpes virus infections. Anti-TNF – antibodies to TNF or soluble TNF receptor that binds TNF, used to treat RA, IBD etc. Associated with TB. Eculizumab – binds C5 and inhibits terminal compliment activation. Increased risk of Neisseria infections. IL-5 inhibitor - Risk for strongyloides

questions.question: Describe the key features of a case-control study, its advantages over a cohort study, and the statistical measure of association obtained from it.

parts.text: Describe the key features of a case-control study, its advantages versus a cohort study, and the statistical result obtained from these studies.

parts_raw.text: What are the key features of a case-control study, what are the advantages vs cohort, what is the statistical result obtained from these studies.

questions.model_answer: Key features: case-control studies are observational and inherently retrospective (data collected before hypotheses formed); participants are selected on the basis of the outcome (cases with the disease, controls without), then investigators look backward in time to compare prior exposures between groups. Advantages over cohort: efficient for uncommon/rare outcomes and diseases with long latency; generally quicker and less costly than following a cohort forward. Statistical result: the odds ratio (whereas cohort studies yield relative risk).

cohort_answer.text:
Retrospective: compares those with outcome + w/o outcomes to see for pertinent exposures
A case control study identifies cases and assesses for exposures associated with the case ie. Occurring more frequently in cases than controls = OR.
Advantages : cases with long latency period/rare diseases
Prospective : exposures known, followed for outcomes, takes longer
Cohorts look at exposures and monitor for cases and compare to a cohort without an exposure ie. Risk of case if exposed vs. not exposed = RR/HR.

parts.text: What does R0 describe?

questions.model_answer: a) R0 (basic reproduction number) is the average number of secondary cases generated by one infectious case introduced into a fully susceptible population. b) Measles (~12-18) > varicella (~10-12) > SARS-CoV-2 (ancestral ~2-3) > 2009 H1N1 (~1.4-1.6) > MERS-CoV (<1). c) The effective/net reproduction number (Rt or Re) is the average number of secondary cases per case in a population that is not fully susceptible (some immunity/intervention present); it reflects transmission at a given time. d) R (or Rt) greater than 1 indicates epidemic growth; R=1 is stable endemic transmission; R<1 indicates decline.

parts.text: Calculate the negative predictive value and positive predictive value in a population with a point prevalence of 1%.
Provide an argument in favour of and one against using this test.

parts_raw.text: Calculate the the NPV and PPV in a population with point prevalence of 1%.
Provide an argument in favor and one against using this test.

questions.model_answer:
a) Take 10,000 people at 1% prevalence: 100 infected, 9900 uninfected.
True positives = 0.99 x 100 = 99; false negatives = 1.
True negatives = 0.99 x 9900 = 9801; false positives = 99.
PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 99/(99+99) = 99/198 = 50%.
NPV = TN/(TN+FN) = 9801/(9801+1) = 9801/9802 = 99.99% (~100%).
So only half of positives are true positives, while a negative essentially excludes infection.

b) In favour: it is a rapid/simple single-visit assay (result in <15-30 min) usable at the point of care with fingerstick or oral fluid and little equipment, which markedly increases the proportion of people who actually receive their result (pregnant women in labour, STI and outpatient clinics, emergency departments) and permits immediate counselling and linkage; with NPV ~100% at this prevalence a nonreactive result reliably rules out established infection.
Against: at 1% prevalence the PPV is only 50%, so half of reactive results are false positives, causing profound patient distress and further testing - no single test is adequate in a low-prevalence population; a reactive result must be followed by a highly specific supplemental assay. Rapid tests are also less sensitive than conventional assays in seroconversion panels (positive 2-8 days later; the fourth-generation rapid assay detects p24 in only ~10%), so acute HIV would be missed.

cohort_answer.text: As prevalence of disease is low NPV is better. For any given test (i.e. sensitivity and specificity remain the same) as prevalence decreases, the PPV decreases because there will be more false positives for every true positive.

questions.model_answer: a) Key features: (1) observational, inherently retrospective study in which participants are selected based on the presence or absence of the outcome, then investigators look backward in time to compare prior exposures between cases and controls; (2) controls are typically matched on baseline variables that influence outcome; (3) prone to recall/selection bias. Advantages over cohort: (1) efficient for rare outcomes (cohort is better for rare exposures); (2) faster, cheaper, smaller numbers, no forward follow-up required. Statistical result: the odds ratio (cohort studies yield relative risk/hazard ratio and incidence).

cohort_answer.text: Key Features: Retrospective (vs potentially prospective for cohort), observational, requires matching; identifies cases based on outcome then assesses for exposures; can be more prone to recall bias. Advantages over Cohort: faster, cheaper, ability to match based on key characteristics, good for rare diseases, fewer individuals needed, no follow-up needed. Statistical Result: Case Control - odds ratio; Cohort - RR or HR, also incidence (less prone to bias)

questions.question: Given a 2x2 table, calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV.
questions.question_raw: Given 2x2 table and told to calculate Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV

parts.text: Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV.

parts_raw.text: Calculate Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV

questions.model_answer: a) Using a 2x2 table (a=TP, b=FP, c=FN, d=TN): Sensitivity = a/(a+c) (proportion of diseased correctly testing positive). Specificity = d/(b+d) (proportion of non-diseased correctly testing negative). PPV = a/(a+b) (probability disease is present given a positive test). NPV = d/(c+d) (probability disease is absent given a negative test). PPV and NPV vary with prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not.
questions.beyond_mandell: Sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV formulas are not detailed in Mandell ch. 52; standard diagnostic-test definitions.

cohort_answer.text: Sensitivity: measures the proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified as such (a/a+c). Specificity: measures the proportion of actual negatives that are correctly identified as such (d/b+d). Positive predictive value (PPV): probability that a person with a positive test truly has the disease (a/a+b). Negative predictive value (NPV): probability that a person with a negative test is truly free from the disease (d/c+d)
